name: Fort Dearborn — root house (b)
aka: the second of the root-houses of the garrison

documented_range.note: The same range and the same single witness as the first mound: attested standing in 1831 by Juliette Kinzie and by nobody else at any date. The range opens with the fort and closes at the final evacuation, because a root house is kept by a garrison; nothing reached follows it further. This record's range is not independent evidence — it is the first mound's, because it is the same sentence.

placement.position_note:
THE COUNT IS KINZIE'S AND THE POINT IS OURS. Kinzie, of 1831: 'The bank of the river which stretches to the west ... was then occupied by the root-houses of the garrison.' ROOT-HOUSES, PLURAL, IS THE ONLY THING ANY SOURCE SAYS ABOUT HOW MANY, and until this record it was the one clause in her sentence the model did not carry: one mound stood for a plural, and `fort_dearborn_root_house`'s own position note said so in as many words. Two is the smallest number that reads her sentence rather than half of it, and it is the number built. NOTHING SUPPORTS A THIRD and none is raised: the plural states a floor and no source, plan or return gives a count, a spacing or a size, so a row of five would be an invention this one is not.

THE POSITION IS A SECOND POINT ON THE SAME BANK TOP, 9.0 m due west of the first, on the stretch Kinzie names and outside the pickets. It is chosen and not derived, exactly as the first one is. WHAT WAS CHECKED, because the first mound had to be moved once for getting this wrong: the committed 1834-harbour-cut heightfield was sampled over this footprint and the ground runs 3.59-3.61 m across it, a fall of 0.02 m, against the 0.85 m fall that displaced the first point in August 2026. The bank's face begins about 6 m further west again (3.42 m at E +1100, 3.21 m at E +1096), so this is the last full footprint the bank top carries before it drops, and a third mound west of it would straddle the fall. EAST is where the fort is: the palisade's west face stands about 13 m east of the first mound, so the pair occupies the whole of the open bank top between the stockade and the drop, which is what 'occupied by the root-houses' describes.

Local E +1108.7, N +235.4. Carry the same uncertainty the first mound carries: the bank is evidence and the point on it is not.
placement.symbolic_location: On the south bank of the Chicago River west of Fort Dearborn, 9 m west of the first root house, on the same bank top between the stockade and the fall.

footprint.note: THE FIRST MOUND'S INVENTED FIGURE, REPEATED RATHER THAN RE-INVENTED. No source gives either cellar a size. 5.0 x 3.6 m is the figure `fort_dearborn_root_house` chose for a cellar big enough to hold a garrison's roots through a winter, and this record takes it unchanged on purpose: a second, different number would be a second invention and would imply a distinction between the two that nothing states.

kind.note: Kinzie names them, in the plural. A root house is a cellar banked over with earth, which is why it reads as a mound rather than as a building.

construction.note: Not stated. Earth banked over a timber-framed cellar is what the type is; what is inferred is the type, not this example.

wall_height_m.note: Unattested. The height of the bank above the surrounding ground.

roof_type.note: Unattested. The archetype builds the mound as a banked truncated pyramid with a plank door in one end; 'flat' names the top of the bank rather than a roof.

chimneys.note: A root house is unheated by definition of the type.

paint.note: The colour of turf and soil. No source describes it.

function.note: Winter storage for the garrison's roots and vegetables, dug into the river bank.

land_owner.value: The ground was entered by John Baptist Baubian, 28 May 1835
land_owner.note: THE UNITED STATES RESERVATION. This is the same tract L108 already derives for `1835_no_build_ground.json` — from G1, Madison's line and the traced waterline — so the polygon is inherited rather than built again, and `check.sh` already re-derives it. The register's own row is the second, independent witness to the date L108 quotes from Andreas: Beaubien's pre-emption, 28 May 1835, five weeks before the scene date. The derived polygon is short of the documented 75.69 acres for the reasons L108 states, and is a floor rather than the reservation. WHETHER THE ENTRY HELD IS NOT READ HERE: it was disputed, and this row records the entry the register carries and nothing about its outcome. THE MARGIN IS ONLY 16 m, which is inside the working horizontal uncertainty of the georeference (about 20 m) doubled, so the grade drops a tier: the tract is right if the constructed line is, and nothing here proves the line to better than that. WHAT THIS ROW CLAIMS AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. It claims that the tract the Illinois State Archives' land-sale register describes contains this structure's committed position — the patent for this ground was ENTERED by this man on this date. It does not claim he still held the ground on 1 July 1835, that he lived here, or that he ever stood on it: a sale is a transaction, and the register's only column about residence names a county. THE SECTION LINES ARE CONSTRUCTED, NOT TRACED (L219): the grid is carried from the single PLSS corner at State & Madison, on the plat's own east-west bearing, in nominal one-mile squares.

citations.citation: Illinois State Archives, Illinois Public Domain Land Tract Sales Database (Springfield: Office of the Secretary of State).
Kinzie, Juliette A. M. Wau-Bun: The 'Early Day' in the North-West. New York: Derby & Jackson, 1856.

research_note: THE PLURAL, BUILT. Kinzie's one sentence is the whole of the evidence for the garrison's root-houses and it is plural; the model carried one mound and said so. This is the second, and with it the sentence is read whole rather than halved. EVERYTHING EXCEPT THE COUNT IS STILL OURS — the point on the bank, the size, the height, the shape — and every one of those is graded reconstructed so that a visitor can see that the pair of mounds is our idea of root houses standing at our idea of two spots. T-1715, the fort's yard ruled.
